spine.thread: Shipping with coding agents. Owning the outcome. Teaching the new workflow.
spine.mantra: Build with agents. Own the outcome.
spine.oneLiner: I build, advise, and teach AI-native software.
spine.support: AI-native software product engineering with coding agents and customer-facing enablement. Based in Switzerland.
spine.why: The red thread through my CV is not a perfect stack and not a list of jobs in order. I worked across all phases of the software development lifecycle.

metaphor.note: The golden cut (Phi Grid + Fibonacci spiral) is the visual and it shows you this: Each step and each turn brings you closer to the goal. But you need to want to make the turn.

pillars.label: Discover
pillars.text: Starting from the need. Clear intent, constraints, and what “done” means — so agents draft against a frame, not a guess.
samples: Defined AI value metrics for a tool at three levels — north star, human adoption, and technical solution fitness.
Owned onboarding and a value-realisation practice for GenAI enterprise search across 50+ data sources and 5 departments.
Agile requirements engineering and business process modelling across various projects in insurance, finance, retail and public transport.

pillars.label: Build
pillars.text: From pilot to production, shipping with coding agents. Investing in automation from the very first step.
samples: GenAI enterprise search (RAG) from pilot to production for 1,000+ users in two months.
Agentic content factory in Python + Agent Skills — curriculum, storyboard, script, slides, video, quality review, deploy.
Agentic Copilot tooling for software testers (test-case generation).

pillars.label: Test
pillars.text: Checking what humans or agents produce before it lands. Automated checks and human review in the loop — nothing ships on trust alone.
samples: Copilot-assisted test-case generation for Swiss luxury retail (~30% coverage).
Quality-review agent plus human approval before a training module goes live.
Spec-driven verification skills in the agent factory loop.

pillars.label: Own
pillars.text: Owning the outcome. The work is not finished when the model answers — it is finished when the outcome holds.
samples: Owned the GenAI search rollout end-to-end — data onboarding through production adoption.
Content factory ships to 1,000+ learners only after the human gate.
Lean-agile delivery in public transport: time-to-market −25%, adoption +30%.

pillars.label: Teach
pillars.text: Teaching the new workflow through enablement and speaking — the same loop I use in production, with a customer-facing trusted advisor posture.
samples: 50+ Copilot / Copilot Studio sessions for 5,000+ practitioners.
Guest lecturer on a Swiss CAS DevOps programme.

surfaces.use-cases: Eight flip cards in four lines, two per category — value realization (metrics, developer experience), flow (idea to product to user feedback), leadership (governance and policy that keep up with fast-changing tools), enablement (training, coaching, sharing what works). Everyday problems teams and leaders face along the software and product development lifecycle when they adopt AI; the problem on the front, how we tackle it on the back. Plain English for mixed readers. No undefined glossary terms.

public: Keep employer and client names off public pages, except the workedWith logo row on the home page.
Do not invent metrics or claims.

cases.name: “What did we get for the money?”
cases.problem: Management asks for results. The only numbers are licence counts and accepted suggestions. Nobody can say if teams ship faster or better, so the budget is at risk.
cases.solution: With the leadership team we agree a few measures that matter: one shared goal, how many people really use the tools, and whether the solution does its job. We take a baseline first, then check against it.

cases.name: Good numbers, unhappy developers
cases.problem: The dashboard shows high usage. Ask the developers and you hear something else: more time fixing generated code, longer reviews, more interruptions. Nobody measures how the work feels.
cases.solution: We put developer experience next to the delivery numbers: a short, regular survey and a few honest conversations. Where the two disagree, we find what gets in the way and fix that first.

cases.name: A new product, and too many ways to start
cases.problem: A team starts a new product from scratch and wants to build it with agents from day one. Which spec-driven approach should we choose? What skills do we need? Weeks go by comparing methods instead of building.
cases.solution: We pick one approach that fits the team and the product, and try it on a first thin slice: write down what is wanted, let agents build against it, check the result. We see which skills are missing, build them as we go, and adjust after the first slice.

cases.name: Faster coding, same delivery speed
cases.problem: Developers write code faster, but changes wait for review, and testing and releases are still manual. The waiting just moved. Features reach users no sooner, and their feedback comes back just as late.
cases.solution: We look at the whole path from idea to product to user feedback and use AI where the waiting is: clearer requirements up front, generated tests, and automatic checks before a person reviews.

cases.name: No clear rules, so AI goes underground
cases.problem: Security and legal have not said what is allowed. Some teams are blocked. Others paste company code into public chatbots. Leaders do not know which is happening where.
cases.solution: I bring engineering, security and legal to one table and we write short, practical rules: which tools, which data, and where a person must check the result. We start with low-risk work and widen step by step.

cases.name: New features every week, a policy from last year
cases.problem: The AI policy took months to approve. Meanwhile the tools bring new features every week: agents, new models, new integrations. The policy does not cover them, so teams wait or decide for themselves.
cases.solution: With leadership we replace the long document with a few lasting principles: which data, which risks, what an agent may do alone, and where a person signs off. A small group reviews what is new on a regular rhythm, and teams know whom to ask.

cases.name: Licences bought, usage flat
cases.problem: The company rolled out AI coding licences. Three months later a few people use them every day, and most tried once and stopped. The training was a feature demo, not their own work.
cases.solution: Hands-on training in the basics, on the team's own code and tickets. We pick two or three everyday tasks, such as tests, docs and small fixes, and agree what to hand over and what to check. Then we follow up on what stuck.

cases.name: What works stays with a few people
cases.problem: A few people have found what really works with AI, and what does not. The rest never hear about it. After the first training nothing follows, and every team makes the same mistakes again.
cases.solution: We make learning a habit: coaching on real work, short regular sessions where teams show what worked and what failed, and hackathons to try new things. Good practices are written down where everyone finds them.
